exam: IISER Aptitude Test (IAT) 2027 preparation — provisional 2026-pattern pilot
title: IAT New Test 4
review_status: fresh AI-assisted authoring; independent academic review pending
notification_source: Official IAT 2026 examination page and 2026 Information Brochure, sections 19 and 23; a 2027 brochure has not been verified
past_paper_reference: 539 English archive entries from 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021–2026; 2026 key provisional; analysed for topic/style only, no questions copied
authoring_source: Fresh original AI-assisted authorship to the 25-test plan and revised IAT instructions; academic review pending
order_policy: fixed authored order; do not shuffle questions or options or renumber image-linked IDs
instructions: This is an original preparation pilot for manual review, based on the verified 2026 scheme; it is not an official IAT paper or a verified 2027 notification.
There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

difficulty_policy.basis: user-directed editorial mix, not measured item difficulty

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A woody plant bears pollen and ovules on separate cones; its ovules are exposed at pollination, although a seed coat develops later. Which observation distinguishes it from an angiosperm?
options: A) Ovules are not enclosed in an ovary before fertilisation
C) Its diploid zygote develops into an embryo
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ovules are not enclosed in an ovary before fertilisation.
Why: Naked ovules on cone scales identify the gymnosperm condition. A subsequent seed coat does not turn the cone into a fruit, which requires an ovary wall.
Why not the others: (B) Pollen, (C) embryos and (D) vascular tissue occur in both seed-plant groups, so each fails the comparison.
Key point: Compare the ovule's enclosure at pollination, not merely the presence of seeds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: The figure depicts a floral section: sepals, petals and stamens arise above the ovary; the ovary has two chambers. If the flower is turned upside down for display, which classification remains valid?
questions.image_alt: Flower section with two ovary chambers below the common level of sepal, petal and stamen attachment.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Inferior, bilocular ovary.
Why: The insertion level of other whorls is above the ovary, defining an epigynous flower with an inferior ovary; a septum divides it into two locules. Rotating a drawing changes its page orientation, not these structural relationships.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) put the attachment below the ovary; (A) and (D) ignore the septum.
Key point: Infer position from attachment, and locule count from internal partitions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Complete hydrolysis of one unbranched peptide releases 18 amino-acid molecules. How many water molecules were consumed if no cyclic bond was present?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 17.
Given: The unbranched chain contains 18 residues.
Formula/Principle: A linear chain of n residues contains n−1 peptide linkages; hydrolysis consumes one water per linkage.
Step 1: Count 18−1=17 bonds.
Step 2: Breaking each bond uses one H₂O, giving 17 molecules.
Why: The terminal residues do not require a bond beyond the chain ends.
Why not the others: (A) counts residues rather than links; (B) subtracts twice; (D) adds a nonexistent terminal bond.
Key point: Distinguish monomer number from linkage number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A tissue consumes 20 mL O₂ and releases 16 mL CO₂ in a short closed-chamber trial. What is its measured respiratory quotient, and which pure-substrate value is it closer to: glucose 1.0 or a typical fat 0.7?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.8, fat.
Given: CO₂ evolved=16 mL and O₂ consumed=20 mL.
Formula/Principle: RQ=volume CO₂/volume O₂ under comparable conditions.
Step 1: RQ=16/20=0.8.
Step 2: Distance to 1.0 is 0.2, while distance to 0.7 is 0.1, so this reading is closer to the fat reference.
Why: The observed ratio may reflect a mixture of substrates; closeness alone does not prove the exclusive substrate.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) invert the ratio; (C) misjudges the closeness.
Key point: Compute the ratio before comparing reference values.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: After a booster dose of the same antigen, serum antibody rises sooner and higher than after the first exposure. Which cellular population most directly explains the difference?
options: A) Long-lived memory B cells selected during the first exposure
B) Mature erythrocytes that bind antigen
C) Platelets that secrete antigen-specific IgG
D) Neutrophils converting into plasma cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Long-lived memory B cells selected during the first exposure.
Why: Priming selects and expands antigen-specific clones. Memory cells respond rapidly on re-exposure and differentiate into antibody-secreting cells, explaining both shorter lag and greater magnitude.
Why not the others: (B) Erythrocytes do not mediate this clonal response; (C) platelets are not antibody producers; (D) neutrophils do not become B-lineage plasma cells.
Key point: The booster changes the available antigen-specific cell population.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In an angiosperm, a fertilised ovule develops normally but the surrounding ovary wall is experimentally removed immediately after fertilisation. Which structure can still arise directly from the ovule?
options: B) Seed with embryo and seed coat
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Seed with embryo and seed coat.
Why: The ovule gives rise to the seed, its integuments form the seed coat, and the zygote forms the embryo. Removal of the ovary wall prevents normal pericarp development, not the ovule's identity.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) describe the ovary-derived fruit wall; (D) is a floral axis, not an ovule derivative.
Key point: Trace seed and fruit structures to different floral precursors.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Selection versus drift in replicate populations
questions.question: An allele begins at frequency 0.10 in eight large replicate populations. After many generations under the same insecticide, it rises above 0.80 in all eight; without insecticide, frequencies fluctuate around 0.10. What is the strongest inference?
options: A) Genetic drift must cause the consistent directional rise
B) Insecticide directly edits the allele in every individual
C) The data support selection favouring the allele under insecticide
D) The allele is necessarily dominant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The data support selection favouring the allele under insecticide.
Why: Parallel directional change across independently maintained large populations under one exposure, together with a no-insecticide comparison, supports differential survival or reproduction. It does not alone prove the molecular mechanism.
Why not the others: (A) Drift is nondirectional across replicates; (B) exposure does not establish directed editing; (D) allele-frequency change does not identify dominance.
Key point: Replication and a control distinguish a selective pattern from chance fluctuations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure shows a simplified malaria cycle with stages P in mosquito salivary glands, Q in human liver cells, R in human red cells and S as gametocytes in human blood. Which stage enters a human with the mosquito bite?
questions.image_alt: Malaria cycle with P in mosquito salivary gland, Q in human liver, R in red cells and S gametocytes in blood; arrow from mosquito to human.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P, sporozoites.
Why: Infected female Anopheles mosquitoes inject salivary-gland sporozoites during feeding. These first reach liver cells, later producing stages that infect erythrocytes; gametocytes are taken up by a subsequent mosquito.
Why not the others: (B) is an intracellular human stage; (C) follows hepatic multiplication; (D) is the sexual precursor ingested from human blood.
Key point: Follow the arrow across hosts before identifying the stage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A plasmid carries antibiotic-resistance genes ampR and tetR; foreign DNA interrupts tetR. Colonies grow on ampicillin but fail to grow on tetracycline. What does this pattern support?
options: A) No plasmid entered the cells
B) A recombinant plasmid disrupted tetR
C) Both resistance genes remain intact
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A recombinant plasmid disrupted tetR.
Why: Growth on ampicillin indicates functional ampR and plasmid uptake; failure on tetracycline indicates loss of tetR activity in the insert-containing construct. The pair of observations provides both positive and negative selection evidence.
Why not the others: (A) predicts ampicillin sensitivity; (C) predicts growth on both drugs; (D) predicts loss of ampicillin growth.
Key point: Interpret the two selective plates together.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Trophic transfer in a simple food chain
questions.question: Producers capture 80,000 kJ; approximately 10% of available energy transfers at each trophic step. What energy reaches tertiary consumers through producers→herbivores→secondary→tertiary consumers?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 80 kJ.
Given: Starting energy=80,000 kJ, with three transfers at 10% each.
Formula/Principle: Available energy after n transfers is initial energy×(0.10)^n.
Step 1: Herbivores receive 8,000 kJ and secondary consumers 800 kJ.
Step 2: Tertiary consumers receive 80 kJ.
Why: The producer-to-tertiary path contains three, not two, trophic transfers.
Why not the others: (A) stops at herbivores; (B) at secondary consumers; (D) adds a fourth transfer.
Key point: Count arrows between trophic levels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A dihybrid testcross yields four phenotype classes of 98, 102, 101 and 99 offspring. Which conclusion best fits these counts?
options: A) Complete linkage of the two loci
B) A 9:3:3:1 ratio from two heterozygotes
C) One locus is lethal in homozygotes
D) Approximate independent assortment of the two loci
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Approximate independent assortment of the two loci.
Why: A double heterozygote crossed to a double recessive reveals its gamete classes directly. Four nearly equal classes fit the 1:1:1:1 expectation; sampling variation explains small deviations.
Why not the others: (A) predicts mainly two parental classes; (B) concerns a dihybrid self, not a testcross; (C) has no support from the four equal counts.
Key point: Match expected ratios to the actual cross design.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two unaffected parents have an affected child with a fully penetrant autosomal recessive condition. Their next child is unaffected. What is the probability that this unaffected child is a carrier?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/3.
Given: Both unaffected parents must be Aa because they produced aa. The child's genotype probabilities are AA=1/4, Aa=1/2, aa=1/4.
Formula/Principle: Conditional probability divides carrier probability by probability of being unaffected.
Step 1: P(unaffected)=3/4.
Step 2: P(Aa | unaffected)=(1/2)/(3/4)=2/3.
Why: The known unaffected status excludes aa before normalising.
Why not the others: (B) is unconditional carrier probability; (C) is homozygote probability; (D) is probability of being unaffected.
Key point: Update the denominator when a phenotype is observed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Heart rate rises from 60 to 90 beats/min while stroke volume falls from 80 to 60 mL/beat. What is the change in cardiac output?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Increase by 0.6 L/min.
Given: Initial HR×SV=60×80 mL/min; final=90×60 mL/min.
Formula/Principle: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.
Step 1: Initial output=4,800 mL/min or 4.8 L/min.
Step 2: Final output=5,400 mL/min or 5.4 L/min; difference=+0.6 L/min.
Why: A fall in stroke volume does not guarantee a fall in total output when rate rises enough.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the sign; (C) uses heart-rate change without the volume change; (D) assumes exact compensation.
Key point: Multiply both changing factors before comparing.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An aquaporin increases water permeability of a membrane without consuming ATP. Which observation is compatible with this channel?
options: A) Water always moves from higher solute concentration to lower
B) Aquaporin pumps solutes against their gradient
C) Net water movement follows a water-potential gradient
D) Transport stops whenever ATP synthesis stops
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Net water movement follows a water-potential gradient.
Why: Aquaporins provide a selective path for passive water transport; direction depends on the water-potential difference across the membrane. A channel can increase the rate without reversing the thermodynamic direction.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the usual osmotic direction; (B) assigns a pump function to a water channel; (D) incorrectly requires ATP for passive flow.
Key point: Separate transport pathway from driving force.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: For one region S=cA^z. Species counts are 20 and 40 at areas A and 4A, respectively. What is z?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/2.
Given: S(4A)/S(A)=40/20=2.
Formula/Principle: In S=cA^z, the ratio for areas 4A and A is 4^z; c cancels.
Step 1: 4^z=2.
Step 2: Because 4^(1/2)=2, z=1/2.
Why: The exponent measures a log–log slope, not the raw species-count change.
Why not the others: (A) predicts a fourfold rise; (B) sixteenfold; (C) only √2-fold.
Key point: Divide paired measurements to eliminate the unknown coefficient.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In the displayed structure CH₂=CH–C≡N, how many σ and π bonds are present, including C–H bonds?
questions.image_alt: Displayed structural formula CH2 double bonded to CH, single bonded to C triple bonded to N.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6 σ and 3 π.
Why: Three C–H links and the C–C, C–C and C–N connections each supply one σ bond, totalling six. The double bond adds one π and the triple bond adds two π.
Why not the others: (B) omits one C–H σ; (C) omits a triple-bond π; (D) misallocates one σ in place of π.
Key point: Each bonded atom pair has exactly one σ bond, regardless of bond order.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A complex ion [M(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ contains neutral NH₃ and chloride ligands. What is M's oxidation state and its coordination number?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) +3, 6.
Given: Four neutral ammonia and two −1 chloride ligands give net charge +1.
Formula/Principle: Oxidation state plus ligand charges equals complex charge; coordination number counts donor atoms.
Step 1: x−2=+1, hence x=+3.
Step 2: Six monodentate ligands supply six donor atoms.
Why: Formal charge and donor count answer different parts of the question.
Why not the others: (A) ignores chloride charge; (C) and (D) count only ammonia donors.
Key point: Count all ligands but include charge only for charged ones.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In one valid Lewis resonance contributor of NO₃⁻ with one N=O and two N–O single bonds, what are the formal charges on N and each singly bonded O?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) N +1; each O −1.
Why: N has four bond-order units and no lone pair, assigning formal +1; a singly bonded O has three lone pairs and formal −1. The doubly bonded O is neutral; the total is −1.
Why not the others: (A) gives net −2; (B) net +1; (C) miscounts N's bonding electrons.
Key point: Check the sum of atom formal charges against ion charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A hydrogen atom in an excited level emits exactly two photons in succession and ends at n=1. Their wavenumbers are R(1/4−1/16) and R(1−1/4), in that order. Which sequence of levels produced them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4→2→1.
Given: Photon wavenumber for nᵢ→n𝒇 is R(1/n𝒇²−1/nᵢ²).
Formula/Principle: Emission lowers the principal quantum number; the photon energy equals the difference of inverse squares.
Step 1: R(1/4−1/16) corresponds to 4→2.
Step 2: R(1−1/4) corresponds to 2→1, consistent with the intermediate state.
Why: A proposed sequence must match both energies and the shared intermediate level.
Why not the others: (B) gives 1/4−1/9 first; (C) ends its first transition at 3; (D) gives 1/4−1/25 first.
Key point: Use both spectral lines as a linked path.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A secondary carbocation can undergo a 1,2-hydride shift to a tertiary carbocation without changing total molecular formula. Which statement best predicts the change?
options: A) It necessarily forms a less stable primary ion
B) The rearrangement can be favourable because hyperconjugation stabilises the tertiary centre
C) Hydride transfer adds a hydrogen atom from solvent
D) A hydride shift changes the net positive charge to negative
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The rearrangement can be favourable because hyperconjugation stabilises the tertiary centre.
Why: The migrating H moves with its electron pair from an adjacent carbon; the cation centre shifts to the carbon that lost H. Greater alkyl substitution commonly stabilises a carbocation.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the stated stability trend; (C) invokes an external source; (D) violates charge conservation.
Key point: Follow the electron pair and compare the two carbocation environments.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which product pair forms when CH₃COCl undergoes complete hydrolysis in water?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) CH₃COOH and HCl.
Why: Water substitutes the acid chloride's Cl at the acyl carbon to give acetic acid; the leaving chloride combines with a proton to give HCl. Carbon skeleton and oxidation state remain those of the acid derivative.
Why not the others: (A) invents an aldehyde and chlorine; (B) breaks the C–C framework; (D) forms a ketone rather than hydrolysing the acyl chloride.
Key point: Hydrolysis replaces the acyl leaving group with OH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An amine reacts with benzenesulfonyl chloride; its sulfonamide product dissolves in aqueous NaOH but reprecipitates upon acidification. Which class of starting amine is indicated?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Primary amine.
Why: A primary amine yields a sulfonamide retaining N–H; base removes that proton to make a water-soluble salt. Acidification regenerates the less soluble neutral sulfonamide.
Why not the others: (B) Secondary-amine sulfonamide lacks N–H and does not show this base solubility; (C) cannot form the same sulfonamide; (D) is permanently charged and not an amine of this class.
Key point: The acid–base behaviour tests whether sulfonamide N–H remains.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Amino acid charge and isoelectric point
questions.question: A neutral-side-chain amino acid has pKₐ(COOH)=2 and pKₐ(NH₃⁺)=9. At pH 6, which form predominates?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻, net 0.
Why: pH 6 lies above the carboxyl pKₐ, so carboxyl is largely deprotonated, but below the ammonium pKₐ, so nitrogen remains largely protonated. Opposite unit charges cancel.
Why not the others: (A) requires more acidic pH; (C) more basic pH; (D) combines protonation states inconsistent with both pKₐ values.
Key point: Compare pH separately with each ionisable group's pKₐ.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure plots ln k against 1/T for reactions X and Y with straight lines of slopes −4000 K and −8000 K respectively. Assuming the same units and Arrhenius behaviour, which has the greater activation energy?
options: A) X, by a factor of two
B) X and Y are equal
C) Slopes alone cannot compare activation energies
D) Y, by a factor of two
questions.image_alt: Two labelled ln k versus inverse-temperature straight lines, X slope negative 4000 K, Y slope negative 8000 K.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Y, by a factor of two.
Why: Arrhenius linearisation gives slope −Eₐ/R for ln k versus 1/T. Y's slope magnitude is twice X's, so its barrier is twice as large when the same R applies. Intercepts affect pre-exponential factors, not the slope comparison.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the slopes; (B) ignores their magnitudes; (C) would apply only without the axis and Arrhenius assumptions.
Key point: Use absolute slope, since the minus sign represents temperature dependence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For AgCl, Ksp=10⁻¹⁰. What is its approximate molar solubility in 0.010 M NaCl, assuming the added chloride dominates dissolved AgCl?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10⁻⁸ M.
Given: Ksp=[Ag⁺][Cl⁻]=10⁻¹⁰ and [Cl⁻]≈10⁻² M.
Formula/Principle: AgCl solubility s equals [Ag⁺] at equilibrium.
Step 1: s×10⁻²≈10⁻¹⁰.
Step 2: s≈10⁻⁸ M, far below 0.010 M, confirming the approximation.
Why: Added common ion suppresses dissolution.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) understate chloride suppression; (D) divides by chloride twice.
Key point: Check the approximation after solving.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Chlorine reacts with cold dilute NaOH to produce Cl⁻ and ClO⁻. Which electron-accounting statement is consistent with the balanced reaction?
options: A) Both chlorine atoms are reduced from 0 to −1
B) One chlorine atom loses one electron while another gains one electron
C) Chlorine's average product oxidation state is +1
D) Oxygen is oxidised from −2 to 0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) One chlorine atom loses one electron while another gains one electron.
Why: Cl starts at 0 in Cl₂; one product chlorine is −1 in chloride, the other is +1 in hypochlorite. The paired one-electron reduction and oxidation balance internally in disproportionation.
Why not the others: (A) neglects hypochlorite; (C) averages −1 and +1 incorrectly; (D) leaves oxygen at −2.
Key point: Assign oxidation states to each chlorine product separately.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Equal masses of the same liquid at 20 °C and 80 °C are mixed in an insulated vessel with negligible heat capacity and no phase change. What is the final temperature?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 50 °C.
Given: Both samples have equal mass and specific heat.
Formula/Principle: Heat lost by hot sample equals heat gained by cold sample.
Step 1: mc(80−T)=mc(T−20).
Step 2: 80−T=T−20, giving T=50 °C.
Why: Equal thermal capacities make the arithmetic midpoint the energy-balance result.
Why not the others: (A) or (B) would require zero change in one sample; (C) gives unequal heat magnitudes.
Key point: The midpoint works only when the heat capacities match.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An ideal liquid mixture contains mole fraction xA=0.25. Pure vapour pressures at this temperature are pA°=80 kPa and pB°=40 kPa. What is A's fraction of the total vapour pressure?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2/5.
Given: xA=.25 and xB=.75.
Formula/Principle: Raoult's law gives pᵢ=xᵢpᵢ°.
Step 1: pA=.25×80=20 kPa; pB=.75×40=30 kPa.
Step 2: Fraction pA/(pA+pB)=20/50=2/5.
Why: Vapour composition differs from liquid composition because pure-component pressures differ.
Why not the others: (A) assumes equal partial pressures; (B) and (C) use an incorrect total or exchange the two vapour shares.
Key point: Calculate both partial pressures before taking a share.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Nitration of toluene gives mostly ortho and para products. What change to the ring substituent would instead favour meta nitration?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Replace CH₃ with NO₂.
Why: Nitro withdraws electron density by resonance and induction, destabilising ortho/para sigma complexes relative to meta attack. Methyl donation instead favours ortho/para substitution.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) donate by resonance and direct ortho/para; (D) is deactivating but still ortho/para directing by lone-pair resonance.
Key point: Direction and overall reaction rate are separate substituent effects.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At room temperature, benzyl chloride undergoes nucleophilic substitution readily, while chlorobenzene resists ordinary SN1/SN2 substitution. Which distinction best explains this?
options: A) Benzyl chloride lacks a C–Cl bond
B) Chlorobenzene forms a more stable phenyl cation than a benzyl cation
C) Chlorobenzene's aryl C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and its carbon is sp²
D) A benzyl carbon cannot undergo backside attack
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Chlorobenzene's aryl C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and its carbon is sp².
Why: Lone-pair conjugation strengthens the aryl bond, ordinary SN2 approach at sp² carbon is disfavoured, and phenyl cation formation is costly. Benzylic carbon is sp³ and its transition states/intermediates can be resonance stabilised.
Why not the others: (A) is false; (B) reverses cation stability; (D) falsely excludes benzylic SN2.
Key point: Compare the carbon bearing chlorine, not simply whether a ring is present.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Hyperbola asymptotes from vertices and focus
questions.question: A hyperbola centred at the origin has transverse vertices (±3,0) and foci (±5,0). Which pair of lines are its asymptotes?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) y=±(4/3)x.
Given: Horizontal transverse axis, a=3 and c=5.
Formula/Principle: For x²/a²−y²/b²=1, c²=a²+b² and asymptotes are y=±(b/a)x.
Step 1: b²=25−9=16, so b=4.
Step 2: Slopes are ±4/3.
Why: The focal distance is not itself the conjugate semiaxis.
Why not the others: (B) swaps a and b; (C) uses c in place of b; (D) mixes b with c.
Key point: Recover the missing semiaxis before finding slope.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Common point of a line family
questions.question: Every line (k+1)x+(2k−1)y=3k+2 passes through one fixed point. What is that point?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (7/3,1/3).
Given: The point must satisfy the equation for every real k.
Formula/Principle: Equate separately coefficients of k and constant terms in an identity.
Step 1: k terms give x+2y=3; constants give x−y=2.
Step 2: y=1/3, x=7/3.
Why: A fixed point must survive any choice of the line parameter, not just one selected k.
Why not the others: (A) misses both equations; (C) satisfies x−y=2 but not x+2y=3; (D) misses the constant equation.
Key point: Separate parameter-dependent and independent parts.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 of (2x+3)/[(x+1)(x+2)] dx.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ln 3.
Given: The denominator factors as (x+1)(x+2).
Formula/Principle: Use partial fractions and evaluate at both bounds.
Step 1: (2x+3)/[(x+1)(x+2)]=1/(x+1)+1/(x+2).
Step 2: [ln(x+1)+ln(x+2)]₀¹=ln2+ln3−ln2=ln3.
Why: Both logarithms contribute boundary terms; the ln2 at the upper bound cancels the ln2 at the lower bound of the other term.
Why not the others: (A) omits a surviving log; (B) integrates only 1/(x+2); (D) omits the lower endpoint.
Key point: Simplify evaluated logarithms before selecting a result.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is the area enclosed by y=x² and y=2x between their intersections?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4/3.
Given: The curves meet at x=0 and x=2.
Formula/Principle: Area is ∫(upper−lower) dx, never a signed cancellation.
Step 1: On (0,2), 2x exceeds x².
Step 2: ∫₀²(2x−x²)dx=[x²−x³/3]₀²=4−8/3=4/3.
Why: The linear curve stays above until the second intersection.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) lose a factor from the interval; (C) drops the subtraction.
Key point: Determine intersections and upper curve first.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Implicit tangent of a level curve
questions.question: For x²+xy+y²=7, the point (1,2) lies on the curve. What is the slope of its tangent there?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −4/5.
Given: x²+xy+y² is constant along the curve.
Formula/Principle: Differentiate implicitly, treating y as a function of x.
Step 1: 2x+y+xy′+2yy′=0, so y′=−(2x+y)/(x+2y).
Step 2: At (1,2), y′=−4/5.
Why: The product xy contributes both y and xy′.
Why not the others: (B) inverts the derivative; (C) misses the sign; (D) drops the x dependence.
Key point: Apply the product rule to xy.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: On integers define aRb when 4 divides (a−b). If the domain is restricted to odd integers, how many equivalence classes remain?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Why: Congruence modulo 4 is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so restriction to a subset preserves those properties. Odd integers fall into residues 1 or 3 modulo 4, both nonempty and distinct.
Why not the others: (A) merges residues 1 and 3; (B) includes even residue classes absent from the domain; (D) mistakes infinitely many members for infinitely many classes.
Key point: Count equivalence classes on the stated domain, not all integers.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let A=[[1,1],[0,1]], B=[[1,0],[1,1]], and AX=B. What is tr(X)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.
Given: AX=B, so X=A⁻¹B, not BA⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: A⁻¹=[[1,−1],[0,1]].
Step 1: A⁻¹B=[[0,−1],[1,1]].
Step 2: Its trace is 0+1=1.
Why: Left multiplication preserves the order dictated by AX=B; matrix multiplication is not commutative.
Why not the others: (A) adds off-diagonal entries; (B) uses the diagonal of B; (C) omits the lower-right entry.
Key point: Solve the matrix equation on the correct side.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed four times. Given that at least one head occurs, what is the probability of exactly two heads?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2/5.
Given: 16 equally likely sequences; one has no heads.
Formula/Principle: P(exactly two | at least one)=P(exactly two)/P(at least one).
Step 1: Six sequences have two heads, while 15 satisfy the condition.
Step 2: Required probability=6/15=2/5.
Why: The conditioning event changes the denominator, not the six favourable sequences.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) retain 16 as denominator; (C) counts an incorrect number of favourable cases.
Key point: Restrict the sample space before forming a ratio.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For acute α and β, tan α=1/2 and tan β=1/3. What is cos(α+β)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/√2.
Given: Acute angles give positive sine and cosine.
Formula/Principle: cos(α+β)=cosα cosβ−sinα sinβ.
Step 1: (cosα,sinα)=(2,1)/√5 and (cosβ,sinβ)=(3,1)/√10.
Step 2: (6−1)/√50=5/√50=1/√2.
Why: Quadrant information fixes the signs, while the subtraction reflects the compound angle.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) omit a term; (D) ignores β.
Key point: Build unit-triangle components before combining angles.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is the foot of the perpendicular from P(2,−3,5) to the xy-plane?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (2,−3,0).
Given: The xy-plane consists of z=0.
Formula/Principle: An orthogonal projection onto that plane changes only the normal (z) coordinate.
Step 1: Keep x=2 and y=−3.
Step 2: Set z=0.
Why: The connecting segment is parallel to the z-axis and perpendicular to the plane.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) change a coordinate within the plane; (C) changes both in-plane coordinates.
Key point: Identify the plane's normal direction.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Cross product from area and orientation
questions.question: Vectors a=(1,2,0) and b=(2,1,0) form two sides of a parallelogram. Which vector gives its oriented area a×b?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (0,0,−3).
Given: Both vectors lie in the xy-plane.
Formula/Principle: The z-component of a×b is aₓbᵧ−aᵧbₓ.
Step 1: 1×1−2×2=−3.
Step 2: The other components vanish, giving −3k̂.
Why: Magnitude 3 is area, but order a×b sets the negative orientation.
Why not the others: (B) reverses order; (C) is in-plane; (D) uses the dot-product sum.
Key point: Preserve operand order in cross products.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Cube roots of unity as geometric points
questions.question: Let ω be a non-real cube root of unity. What is |1−ω|²?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3.
Given: ω=−1/2±i√3/2, a vertex of the unit-circle equilateral triangle.
Formula/Principle: |z|²=z z̄, or sum of squared real and imaginary parts.
Step 1: 1−ω=3/2∓i√3/2.
Step 2: Modulus squared=9/4+3/4=3.
Why: Both non-real conjugate choices have the same distance from 1.
Why not the others: (A) uses |ω|²; (B) omits the real shift; (D) would correspond to opposite unit-circle points.
Key point: Geometric distance is invariant under conjugation here.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For which real t does x²−tx+4=0 have two distinct positive real roots?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) t>4.
Given: Product of roots=4>0 and sum=t.
Formula/Principle: Distinct real roots require discriminant t²−16>0; positive sum selects positive rather than negative roots.
Step 1: Real distinct gives t<−4 or t>4.
Step 2: Positive sum removes t<−4, leaving t>4.
Why: At t=4 the two positive roots coincide, violating distinctness.
Why not the others: (A) admits non-real roots; (B) includes the double root; (C) gives two negative roots.
Key point: Combine discriminant and Vieta signs with strict endpoints.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Optimising a constant-term coefficient across exponents
questions.question: For positive integer p in {1,2,4,10}, which p makes the constant-term coefficient of (x²+x^(−p))⁶ largest?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.
Given: Choosing r factors of x^(−p) gives power 2(6−r)−pr=12−(p+2)r.
Formula/Principle: A constant term needs integer r=12/(p+2) between 0 and 6; its coefficient is C(6,r).
Step 1: For p=1,2,4,10, the allowed r values are 4,3,2,1.
Step 2: Corresponding coefficients are 15,20,15,6, so p=2 gives the maximum.
Why: Exponent cancellation alone does not determine which of several valid expansions has the largest coefficient.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) each give 15; (D) gives 6.
Key point: Compare the binomial coefficients only after finding each admissible constant term.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The infinite geometric series 1+r+r²+⋯ has a finite sum for which condition on real r?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) |r|<1.
Why: The nth partial sum is (1−rⁿ)/(1−r) for r≠1. It approaches 1/(1−r) only when rⁿ→0, precisely for −1<r<1; r=1 grows and r=−1 oscillates.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) each admit ratios of magnitude at least one; (C) incorrectly includes both boundary values.
Key point: Test endpoints rather than silently extending a finite-series formula.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Voltage and current are measured independently with maximum percentage uncertainties 2% and 1%. For R=V/I, what is the maximum first-order percentage uncertainty in R?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3%.
Given: Fractional maximum bounds are 0.02 in V and 0.01 in I.
Formula/Principle: First-order worst-case relative errors add for a quotient.
Step 1: δR/R≈δV/V−δI/I as signed perturbations.
Step 2: Maximum magnitude≤2%+1%=3%.
Why: Opposite signed errors can reinforce in the quotient; subtracting percentages is not a safe upper bound.
Why not the others: (B) ignores current; (C) ignores voltage; (D) multiplies percentage numbers.
Key point: Distinguish worst-case uncertainty from a specific signed deviation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal rough floor with μs=0.4. Taking g=10 m/s², what horizontal force first reaches the limiting static friction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 20 N.
Given: Normal reaction=mg=50 N on the horizontal floor.
Formula/Principle: Limiting static friction fₛ,max=μsN.
Step 1: fₛ,max=.4×50=20 N.
Step 2: At the threshold the applied force balances this maximum.
Why: Static friction adjusts to smaller forces before its limit is reached.
Why not the others: (A) halves the result; (C) uses N itself; (D) omits the mass factor.
Key point: Use the limiting value only at impending motion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two wires of equal length L and cross-section A, with Young moduli Y and 2Y, are joined end to end and pulled by force F. What is their combined extension?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3FL/(2AY).
Given: Both series wires carry the same tension F.
Formula/Principle: Each extension equals FL/(AYᵢ); series extensions add.
Step 1: First wire extends FL/(AY), second FL/(2AY).
Step 2: Sum=3FL/(2AY).
Why: Equal force does not imply equal strain for different moduli.
Why not the others: (A) retains only the stiffer wire; (B) only the first; (C) assumes identical moduli.
Key point: Add displacements for elements in series.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Differential thermal expansion in a ring-gap arrangement
questions.question: In the figure, a metal sphere just fits through a circular hole in a metal plate at 20 °C. Both are heated equally; the sphere's expansion coefficient is twice the plate's. What happens for a small temperature rise?
options: A) The hole contracts while the sphere grows
B) Both sizes grow at exactly the same fractional rate
C) The sphere can no longer pass through the hole
D) The hole grows twice as fast fractionally
questions.image_alt: Sphere and plate hole have matching initial diameter d; sphere coefficient 2 alpha and plate coefficient alpha.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The sphere can no longer pass through the hole.
Why: A hole expands as if it were made of the plate material; its diameter scales by approximately 1+αΔT, while the sphere diameter scales by 1+2αΔT. Starting equal, the sphere becomes larger.
Why not the others: (A) falsely makes a heated hole contract; (B) ignores the specified coefficients; (D) reverses their ratio.
Key point: Apply each material's linear expansion to its own diameter.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A rigid insulated container holds one mole of ideal diatomic gas with vibrational modes inactive. A paddle does 5RT₀/2 work on gas initially at T₀, with no heat transfer. What is final temperature?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2T₀.
Given: Diatomic gas has five active quadratic degrees of freedom, n=1, and work on gas=5RT₀/2.
Formula/Principle: U=(5/2)nRT and first law ΔU=Q+W_on.
Step 1: Q=0 and ΔU=(5/2)R(Tf−T₀)=5RT₀/2.
Step 2: Tf−T₀=T₀, hence Tf=2T₀.
Why: Mechanical stirring raises internal energy despite the container being thermally insulated.
Why not the others: (A) halves the temperature rise; (B) mistakes work in units RT for final T; (C) doubles the rise.
Key point: Insulated means Q=0, not ΔU=0.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A small-amplitude pendulum is lengthened from L to 1.44L while g stays fixed. What is the ratio of new to old period?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.20.
Given: Lnew/Lold=1.44.
Formula/Principle: T=2π√(L/g) for a simple pendulum at small amplitude.
Step 1: Tnew/Told=√1.44.
Step 2: Ratio=1.20.
Why: Period varies with square root of length rather than length itself.
Why not the others: (A) uses direct proportionality; (C) takes reciprocal; (D) squares length ratio.
Key point: Cancel common factors before taking the square root.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An unknown tone gives 4 beats/s with 256 Hz and 8 beats/s with 260 Hz. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 252 Hz.
Given: |f−256|=4 and |f−260|=8.
Formula/Principle: Beat frequency is the absolute difference of two close frequencies.
Step 1: First reference permits f=252 or 260 Hz.
Step 2: Against 260 Hz, these give 8 or 0 beats/s; only 252 qualifies.
Why: One beat count alone has a high/low ambiguity.
Why not the others: (B) gives 8 beats against 256; (C) gives none against 260; (D) gives none against 256.
Key point: Intersect candidate sets from two reference tones.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.sub_topic: Potential difference across a uniform field
questions.question: In 0<x<2 m a uniform electric field is +3 V/m along x. If V(0)=10 V, what is V(2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4 V.
Given: Eₓ=+3 V/m over 2 m.
Formula/Principle: ΔV=−∫Eₓ dx.
Step 1: V(2)−V(0)=−3×2=−6 V.
Step 2: V(2)=10−6=4 V.
Why: Electric potential decreases along the field direction for positive E.
Why not the others: (A) reverses sign; (B) ignores field; (C) uses only one metre.
Key point: Keep the minus sign between field and potential gradient.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A wire with carrier density n and drift speed v has current density J. A second wire has carrier density n/2 and drift speed 2v, with the same charge magnitude. What is its current density?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) J.
Given: n′=n/2 and v′=2v.
Formula/Principle: Drift current-density magnitude J=nqv.
Step 1: J′=(n/2)q(2v).
Step 2: Factors cancel, so J′=J.
Why: Fewer carriers can yield the same flow per area if each drifts proportionally faster.
Why not the others: (A) divides twice; (C) changes only v; (D) compounds two increases that are not both present.
Key point: Current density depends on the product of density and drift speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal inductor stores energy U at current I. Its current is first doubled, then the inductance is halved while current remains doubled. What is the final energy in units of U?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2U.
Given: Final L′=L/2 and I′=2I.
Formula/Principle: Magnetic energy U=(1/2)LI².
Step 1: Doubling I alone multiplies energy by four.
Step 2: Halving L at that current halves 4U to 2U.
Why: Energy depends quadratically on current but linearly on inductance; compare the final state with the initial one.
Why not the others: (A) changes only L; (B) treats effects as cancelling linearly; (D) ignores the L change.
Key point: Apply both changes to the same energy expression.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The figure compares current amplitude versus driving frequency for series RLC circuits P and Q with the same L and C. P has a taller, narrower resonance peak than Q. Which is consistent?
options: A) P has greater resistance and greater bandwidth
B) P has greater resistance but smaller bandwidth
C) Both necessarily have different resonance frequencies
D) P has smaller resistance and smaller bandwidth
questions.image_alt: Two current versus driving-frequency resonance curves centred at the same frequency; P is taller and narrower than Q.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P has smaller resistance and smaller bandwidth.
Why: At series resonance impedance is R, so peak current V/R is larger for smaller R. Bandwidth in angular frequency is R/L, so the same smaller R narrows the peak with L fixed.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) predict a shorter peak for greater R; (C) conflicts with the common L and C setting the same ideal resonance.
Key point: Read both peak height and width, not one feature alone.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Prism minimum deviation and refractive index
questions.question: A prism has angle 60° and minimum deviation 30° in air. What is its refractive index?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) √2.
Given: Prism angle A=60°, minimum deviation δm=30°.
Formula/Principle: n=sin[(A+δm)/2]/sin(A/2).
Step 1: Numerator sin45°=1/√2 and denominator sin30°=1/2.
Step 2: Ratio=√2.
Why: At minimum deviation the two refractions are symmetric, giving the stated formula.
Why not the others: (B) uses an incorrect refraction angle; (C) neglects sin45°; (D) inverts the ratio.
Key point: Half both the sum and the prism angle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A film of refractive index n lies between air and a glass substrate of index greater than n. At normal incidence, what condition gives constructive interference of the two principal reflected rays, neglecting additional reflections?
options: A) 2nt=(m+1/2)λ₀ because one reflection reverses phase
B) 2nt=mλ₀ because both reflections reverse phase
D) Every thickness gives destructive reflection
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2nt=mλ₀ because both reflections reverse phase.
Why: Reflection from air to film and from film to higher-index glass each adds a π phase reversal, so their relative reflection phase is zero. The remaining round-trip optical path is 2nt and must equal an integer free-space wavelength.
Why not the others: (A) assumes only one reversal; (C) omits the round trip and index; (D) ignores path-dependent phase.
Key point: Count relative, not absolute, reflection phase changes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Electron de Broglie wavelength under acceleration
questions.question: Nonrelativistic electrons accelerated from rest through V have wavelength λ. What wavelength results from acceleration through 4V?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) λ/2.
Given: Electron charge and mass are unchanged; kinetic energy eV.
Formula/Principle: λ=h/√(2meV) in the nonrelativistic limit.
Step 1: Voltage grows by factor four, so momentum grows by √4=2.
Step 2: Wavelength halves.
Why: Accelerating potential sets kinetic energy, not momentum directly.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) increase λ with voltage; (D) scales λ inversely with V rather than √V.
Key point: Keep the square-root dependence.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal half-wave rectifier sends v(t)=V₀ sinωt to a resistor R during the positive half-cycle and zero otherwise. What is average resistor power over a full cycle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) V₀²/(4R).
Given: Power=v²/R for half a cycle and zero for half a cycle.
Formula/Principle: Average sin² over a positive half-cycle is 1/2.
Step 1: Mean over that active half-cycle is V₀²/(2R).
Step 2: Only half the full period is active, yielding V₀²/(4R).
Why: Mean power uses squared voltage, not the square of average voltage.
Why not the others: (A) uses peak power; (B) averages only the conducting half; (D) introduces an extra factor two.
Key point: Average over the full period.
